compressed-gas-intro.title: Introduction to Compressed Gas Hazards
compressed-gas-intro.content: Compressed gas cylinders store gas under high pressure, making them potentially dangerous if damaged, mishandled, or connected improperly. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.101 governs compressed gases in general industry. Different gases carry different hazards: some are flammable, some are toxic, some are oxidizers, and some — even "inert" ones like nitrogen, argon, or helium — can displace oxygen and create suffocation hazards. Cryogenic liquids add cold-burn and rapid-expansion hazards. Always review the SDS before working with an unfamiliar gas.

gas-storage-identification.title: Cylinder Identification: Labels, Tags, and Safety Data Sheets
gas-storage-identification.content: The only reliable way to identify the contents of a compressed gas cylinder is by reading its label or tag. Never rely on paint color — cylinder colors are not standardized for gas identification and can be misleading. Before using any cylinder, verify its contents by reading the label, then review the Safety Data Sheet for hazard information, PPE requirements, storage guidance, and emergency procedures. If a label is missing, damaged, or unreadable, do not use the cylinder — report it to a supervisor immediately.

gas-hazard-categories.title: Compressed Gas Hazard Categories
gas-hazard-categories.content: Compressed gases fall into several hazard categories: flammable gases (hydrogen, propane, acetylene) can ignite near sparks or flames; oxidizers (oxygen, fluorine) intensify combustion; toxic gases (carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulfide, chlorine) can poison workers at low concentrations; corrosive gases can damage skin, eyes, and respiratory tissue; and inert gases (nitrogen, argon, helium) can displace oxygen without warning, causing unconsciousness or death. Cryogenic liquids produce extremely cold temperatures and can rapidly expand into large gas volumes.

cylinder-storage-security.title: Safe Cylinder Storage and Security
cylinder-storage-security.content: Cylinders must be stored upright, secured with a proper chain, strap, rack, or stand — not just a loosely draped chain. Storage areas must be cool, dry, and well-ventilated. Flammable gases and oxidizers must be separated by at least 20 feet or a suitable fire-rated barrier to reduce fire and explosion risk. Keep cylinders away from ignition sources including sparks, open flames, smoking areas, and hot work operations. Valve protection caps must be in place whenever cylinders are stored and not connected for use.

cylinder-handling-movement.title: Handling and Moving Compressed Gas Cylinders
cylinder-handling-movement.content: Never drag, roll by hand over long distances, or drop cylinders. Use a cylinder cart or hand truck, and secure the cylinder to the cart before moving. Keep the valve protection cap in place during transport — it protects the valve if the cylinder falls. If a cylinder begins to fall, do not try to catch it; move clear and report the incident. Never lift a cylinder by its cap, valve, or regulator. Wear required PPE including safety footwear when handling cylinders.

connections-leak-checks.title: Connecting Cylinders and Checking for Leaks
connections-leak-checks.content: Verify that the regulator, fitting, hose, and system are designed for the specific gas before connecting. Never force mismatched connections or use unauthorized adapters — a fitting that does not fit may be preventing a dangerous mismatch. Open valves slowly and stand to the side of the regulator. After connecting, check for leaks using an approved leak-detection solution — never use a flame. Bubbles at a fitting indicate a leak; close the valve, alert the supervisor, and follow site procedure before continuing.

emergency-response.title: Emergency Response and Evacuation for Gas Leaks
emergency-response.content: If a compressed gas leak occurs, alert nearby workers and supervisors. Near flammable gas leaks, do not operate electrical switches — any arc can ignite the gas. Do not enter a leak area unless you are trained, authorized, and properly equipped with required respiratory protection or SCBA. Follow the facility emergency action plan, move to the assembly area, and do not re-enter until authorized. The SDS provides emergency response guidance including first aid, firefighting, and accidental release measures. Report all leaks, releases, and near misses.
